title: Year one close
hook: from the top of the first mountain, you can see the next ones: the Upanishads, the Ramayana, the Yoga Sutras, your track

segments.voice: Yesterday: shikhara, the whole year in one sit. Words, stories, practices, the Gita, the depths, all held at once. Your line was look how far. Did you tell someone one thing you know now? Day three hundred thirty-one.

There's a second thing that happens at the top of a mountain, a minute after the first. You've turned around and looked at the trail. You've caught your breath. And then you turn back the other way, and you see it. Behind this peak, there's another. And behind that one, a whole line of them, blue and white and going on past where your eyes can follow. The first mountain was the one you could see from the parking lot. The ranges were hiding behind it the whole time. This is the last day of year one. Today we look at what's ahead.
screen: `THE SECOND MINUTE AT THE TOP.` → `ANOTHER PEAK, THEN ANOTHER.` → `THE LAST DAY OF YEAR ONE.`

segments.voice: Start with where you stand. Year one gave you the vocabulary, the stories, the practices, one complete scripture read in order, and a first look at the depths. That's a real thing. You didn't sample the Gita; you read it straight through, in order. Now look ahead. The first range is the rest of the principal Upanishads. You met four of them this year. Year two opens the others, beginning tomorrow with the Chandogya and its teaching on om, which it calls the essence of essences. Later in that range you'll reach lines Hindus still quote, like the Chandogya's tat tvam asi: you are that. The second range is the Ramayana again, but this time as a year-long serial, the full story, slowly, the way families once heard it over many evenings. The third is the Yoga Sutras complete: all one hundred ninety-five short threads of Patanjali, not just the opening. Then your lineage track in full, whichever you walked. And behind those, farther off: the Mahabharata as a serial, the Puranas, the saints and poets from the Alvars to Kabir to Vivekananda. Nobody climbs all of that in a week, and the texts themselves don't pretend you would. The Katha Upanishad, which you read this year, tells the seeker to arise, awake, and learn from those who know, and it says the path is as sharp as a razor's edge and hard to cross. It never says the path is short. It says to get up, wake up, and find someone who knows the way. There's more. There's always more.
screen: `WHERE YOU STAND: THE FIRST MOUNTAIN.` · `THE REST OF THE UPANISHADS.` · `THE RAMAYANA, THE YOGA SUTRAS, YOUR TRACK.` · `ARISE, AWAKE: THE PATH IS LONG.` · then, large: `THE RANGES AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Last sit of year one. Sit tall, like someone at the top of a hill. Breathe in, and feel what you carry now that you didn't carry a year ago: a word, a story, a habit, a question. Breathe out, and let it settle. Then turn, in your mind, toward the ranges. You don't have to know how you'll climb them. Just see them there, waiting, patient as mountains are. If you pray, you can bring your own thanks for the year. The bell holds the time.
Himalaya, the abode of snow. The great range still ahead: the rest of the Upanishads, the Ramayana as a serial, the Yoga Sutras complete, your lineage track in full, and farther peaks behind them.
Your line: there's more. There's always more. Today, before you sleep, name one thing from this year you want to understand better next year. That's day three hundred thirty-one, and year one.

howItsDone: Hindu study is traditionally lifelong: people return to the Upanishads, the epics and the Gita again and again, often with a teacher, and many families hear the Ramayana or the Bhagavata Purana recited over days or weeks.

fork.setup: you've reached the top of the first mountain and seen the ranges behind it. what do you do tomorrow?
options: take one more small step, the way you took every other.
try to climb every range at once.
fork.reveal: the whole year was one step a day. the ranges are climbed the same way, starting tomorrow with the Chandogya.

original.note: Sanskrit himālaya: hima, snow, + ālaya, abode: the abode of snow, the great range.

trapdoor: what you thought: year one is the course, and now it's over.
what it means: year one is the first mountain; the ranges, the rest of the texts, start tomorrow.
what a scholar hears: the Katha's arise, awake (1.3.14) became a watchword of Swami Vivekananda, who made it a call to a whole generation.

notes: Year one close. The ranges are named from the outline ('THE RANGES' section and day 332's Chandogya opening); if the year-two order changes, update this day.

Katha 1.3.14 paraphrased (Müller's 1884 wording not on the validator's list, so not quoted). Reviewer changed 'Hindus have quoted for three thousand years' to 'for well over two thousand years': the Chandogya is usually dated to the first millennium BCE, perhaps 8th–6th century, and dates are debated.
Yoga Sutras: 195 sutras in the common count (some editions 196). Vivekananda's use of 'arise, awake' as a watchword: confirm.
Carry kept exactly as the index ('there's more. there's always more.'), including its internal period.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'many people meet the Gita through its best-loved verses', 'one of the oldest and longest' and 'quoted for well over two thousand years' cut (sweeping claim, superlatives and a date not in the cited texts; the earlier review's two-thousand-year fix is superseded); 'the Hindu tradition has never pretended' softened; the stock 'not a warning, an invitation' ending replaced with the Katha's own instruction.
